Lessons.Title: Measure to Find the Area — Measure Real Rectangles and Build Assigned Areas
ExplanationParagraphs: First edition 2021 IM K–5 Grade 3 Unit 2 Lesson 9, CCSS 3.MD.C.7.b. The lesson moves from invisible gridlines to MEASURING real rectangle sides with a ruler, multiplying side lengths, and physically creating tape-bordered rectangles of prescribed SQUARE-FOOT area. Grade 3 source learner PDF has three pages. Source instructional order: 10-minute Notice and Wonder, 15-minute rectangle measuring, 20-minute hands-on rectangle construction, synthesis, 5-minute gated source Cool-down.

Warm-up: two visually corresponding publisher dot illustrations show SIX groups of THREE dots, with 15 black dots plus three newly added blue dots. In the first diagram the sixth group is separate; in the second the new group is represented as an extra column of the same rectangular array. The math is 5×3+1×3=18=6×3. Notice an additional group of three rather than just recounting isolated dots. Edulytics should draw independent versions of these models, not reproduce source colored pixels.

Activity 1 'Measure to Find Area' (15 min): the source first-edition 2021 Student Task Statements PDF page 2 presents three UNGRIDDED rectangles A, B and C. The original publisher SVG geometry gives exact NOMINAL ruler dimensions using 28.3465 SVG points per centimeter: A 170.08×85.04 points = 6×3 cm, area 18 cm²; B 113.39×141.73 points = 4×5 cm, area 20 cm²; C 283.47×85.04 points = 10×3 cm, area 30 cm². Students must first predict which is largest (C), then use a ruler accurately aligned to 0 on a full-size printed version, measure each SIDE and compute its area with units. Edulytics separately makes original instructional geometry with proportional CSS outlines labelled as conceptual dimensions; do NOT use CSS physical screen length or an arbitrarily scaled printer as a reference centimeter ruler. The 2021 source ruler image has whole centimeter ticks with subdivisions, not one centimeter for every small tick. Teachers validate physically measured source A/B/C on actual paper.

Activity 2 'Create a Rectangle': classroom physical team assignment of ONE of six area targets 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 16 SQUARE FEET. Teams of four use painter's/masking tape, inch rulers and yardsticks to mark the correct real floor rectangle. Each team explains factor pairs, measures side lengths in FEET, checks every side and interior covered area, and records a diagram and justification. Possible side pairs (not unique answers): 2×2 for 4, 2×3 for 6, 3×3 for 9, 2×5 for 10, 3×4 for 12 and 4×4 for 16. Source teacher preparation requires ONE roll of masking/painter's tape per group of four. No machine result can certify tape placement, side measurement or group collaboration.

MLR8 Discussion Supports: give groups a few minutes to ensure every student can explain the constructed area and have them rehearse explanations before presenting. Engagement: Develop Effort and Persistence uses supportive group questions for equitable collaboration. The original student p2 A/B/C measurement is scored by a teacher who sees the original correctly scaled printed sheet; any optional independent Edulytics rectangles with GIVEN dimensions are separate numeric practice, never falsely labelled the original A/B/C's measurements.

Lesson synthesis compares earlier full grids, partial grids and NO-grid rectangles to argue that ruler-measured side lengths are enough to compute area. Distinguish centimeters from square centimeters in Activity 1, and feet from SQUARE feet in Activity 2. Do not transfer square-inch or square-centimeter area answers across different units without conversion. Publisher original educator-gated 'Find the Area' Cool-down is not reproduced; Edulytics has an independently authored goal-equivalent item.

Source 2021 PDF p2 original shape vector geometry can be verified from actual publisher SVG dimensions independently of printing: A=18 cm², B=20 cm², C=30 cm² at intended print scale, so C is largest. These quantities are grounded source authoring references rather than a claim that an arbitrary viewer/printer shows correct physical centimeters. The first-party digital tasks explicitly label nominal source dimensions, while measuring and drawing are teacher reviewed.

To measure a real rectangle physically, put the ruler's zero mark at ZERO against the starting edge and read the two side lengths in centimeters. Never infer printed physical centimeters from uncalibrated screen pixels; teacher verifies measurements.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measure both side lengths
KeyConcepts.Definition: You can find a rectangle's area using the length and width even when no squares are visible.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a zero-aligned ruler to measure both sides in the same linear unit, multiply, and report the matching square unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 7-cm by 4-cm first-party rectangle has area 28 cm².

KeyConcepts.Title: Physical scale matters
KeyConcepts.Definition: Original source SVG nominal vector geometry has real intended centimeter scale, while browser CSS and printer scaling may distort physical lengths.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Nominal correct-source measurements A 6×3, B 4×5, C 10×3 cm must be checked against the student's own actual print/ruler alignment; never claim the web display is a physical ruler.
KeyConcepts.Example: The nominal source C rectangle measures 10 cm by 3 cm for area 30 cm², but scaling a printout to 50% would halve its actual measured sides.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compose an assigned area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given a target in square feet, select side-length factors and build a floor rectangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Product of actual side lengths in FEET must equal the assigned area in square feet.
KeyConcepts.Example: 12 ft² may be 3 ft by 4 ft, or 2 ft by 6 ft.

KeyConcepts.Title: Communicate the array interpretation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding one 3-dot group changes five groups of three to six groups of three.
KeyConcepts.Example: Separate equal groups and rectangular dots can represent the same product.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up two independent group models
WorkedExamples.Question: How can an additional colored 3-dot group make six groups of three?
WorkedExamples.Method: Recognize five old groups and one new group.
Steps: Five groups of three have 5×3=15 dots.
Add one more group of three blue dots.
A 6-by-3 array represents the same total.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks structure and groups, not color copying.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent ruler-length example
WorkedExamples.Question: A separate first-party rectangle measures 7 cm by 4 cm. What is its area?
Steps: Check ruler begins at the zero tick.
Record length 7 cm and width 4 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is independently authored practice and NOT a source A/B/C numerical key.

WorkedExamples.Title: Create a taped rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Your group is assigned exactly 12 square feet. Describe one valid construction.
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose integer factors and mark real feet on floor.
Steps: Select one possible pair: 3 ft by 4 ft.
Mark physical adjacent sides with a ruler/yardstick.
Tape straight lines to complete the rectangle.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One feasible plan is 3 ft × 4 ft = 12 ft², among other valid orientations/factors.
WorkedExamples.Check: Only classroom teacher validates physical build.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three original source rectangles A–C
WorkedExamples.Question: What are the intended centimeter areas of original A, B and C, and which is largest?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the original SVG geometry and verify via physical centimeters in the full-size 2021 printout.
Steps: Original source A is 6 cm across and 3 cm tall: 6×3=18 cm².
Original source B is 4 cm across and 5 cm tall: 4×5=20 cm².
Original source C is 10 cm across and 3 cm tall: 10×3=30 cm².
Predict and verify that source C covers the most space.
Students' measured dimensions must be checked by teacher using a correctly scaled printout and ruler zero.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A = 18 cm²; B = 20 cm²; C = 30 cm²; C is greatest.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check source vector scale and the student's physical ruler setup; optional answer anchors do not certify a ruler measurement.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing shape C only because it is tall, without measuring it.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Height is just one of two needed side lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Starting the ruler at its plastic edge instead of zero mark.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An offset measurement yields incorrect area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Line up the zero mark with one endpoint.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Giving a 12 ft² assigned team a taped shape enclosing 12 linear feet of perimeter instead.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check inside region with 3×4 one-square-foot units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating SVG coordinate units or display pixels as physical centimeters without scaling.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original SVG vectors are drafted at an intended 28.3465pt/cm, but a zoomed browser or rescaled print changes measured physical size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Source nominal A 6×3 (18 cm²), B 4×5 (20 cm²), C 10×3 (30 cm²); pupils measure with an actual cm ruler on 100% paper or explicitly given dimensions.

SummaryPoints: Original source three-page PDF; two group/array warm-up diagrams both 18 dots (15 black and 3 blue).
2021 source p2: measured intended A=6×3=18 cm², B=4×5=20 cm², C=10×3=30 cm². Original SVG viewBox geometry verified; correct print scale and actual ruler measurement remain teacher observed.
2021 source p3: students form ONE assigned rectangle from 4,6,9,10,12,16 ft² using tape and real foot lengths in teams of four, then explain.
First-party numeric examples with given dimensions remain clearly separate from source print measurement and taped builds.
MLR8 collaborative oral rehearsal and teacher review of measurement and construction remain mandatory.
No publisher source art re-used; no tests/CI/Stage D/academic approval performed.
Six source Activity 2 physical assignment alternatives: 4, 6, 9, 10, 12 or 16 ft² — one per group, not one student doing all six. Tape placement and explanation graded only by teacher.
